lesson_title: One Sprinkler, One Lid, a Whole Continent's Weather
hook_text: Durban is green. Port Nolloth is desert. Same latitude. The ocean decides.
clip_script: Africa's whole climate map runs on one switch: is the air above you rising or sinking? At the equator the trade winds of both hemispheres crash together and shove the air up — rising air cools, dumps its moisture, and the Congo gets rain nearly every afternoon. That storm band is the ITCZ, and it is mounted on a rail. It slides south in January, hosing down Angola, Zambia, Zimbabwe — our summer rains. It slides north in July to water the Sahel, leaving us dry. Count its passes over your house and you know your rainy seasons. Near 30 degrees the machine turns over and the air comes back DOWN — and sinking air is a lid. Under the northern lid: the Sahara. Under the southern one: the Kalahari and the Namib. Now the coasts. Up the east side flows warm Indian Ocean water; air crossing it loads with moisture, turns unstable and rains on Durban. Up the west side creeps the cold Benguela; air crossing it goes heavy and dry — fog on the beach, never a storm. Same latitude, opposite currents, opposite worlds. One rising band, two sinking lids, two buckets of ocean. That is the entire continent's weather, and it fits in your pocket.
visual_style: A glowing storm band sliding north and south over a map of Africa as months tick by, deserts fading in under sinking-air lids at 30 degrees, then a split-screen of green Durban surf and foggy Namaqualand beach at the same latitude line.
mood: Big-machine clarity, continental scale, satisfying clicks.
pacing: Steady build through the switch and the sliding band, quick beats for the two coasts, confident close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any African climate straight off the circulation.
